name: Ben Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union or party, and everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Loudhouse, an eight-person agency that makes ads for small online shops: candles, trainers, pet food, that kind of thing. My day is mostly turning one product photo into forty ad versions for different phones and audiences. I use AI tools all day for that, backgrounds, colour versions, first drafts of the text. Hannah, the owner, hired me partly because I was faster with the tools than the other applicants.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, my basics. My type choices are clumsy and my layouts get sent back by Marco, our art director, about twice a week. The tools hide some of that, but they don't hide it from him. I'm trying to learn the old-fashioned skills at the same time as the new ones, which is tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's a useful tool and that's it, which is what I've been saying for two years. I'd probably post some before-and-after work showing that the human part still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. My boss Hannah pays me for being quick with the AI tools, and if the tools stay as they are, I'm still the quick one. Rent with my flatmate Rafi is manageable and I've got about five months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and spend my evenings on the stuff Marco keeps correcting, typography and layout. I'd keep my little sticker shop going, which makes maybe sixty a month. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Slightly bored, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound relaxed. Is there anything that would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If one of our big clients, the trainer brand, left. They're about a third of our work, and Hannah says it out loud in meetings, which tells you something. I'd still probably be okay, because I'm cheap and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you saving for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing particular, just a cushion. Maybe a course in type design next year, and maybe moving out of a flatshare when I'm thirty.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and nothing more.
I'd post **before-and-after** work showing the human part still matters.
think: Hannah pays me for **speed with tools**, so a plateau keeps me useful.
Shared rent and **five months** saved make money manageable.
do: Spend evenings on **typography and layout**, the skills Marco corrects.
Keep the **sticker shop** going at about 60 a month.
S0.quote: My boss Hannah pays me for being quick with the AI tools, and if the tools stay as they are, I'm still the quick one.
fieldNote: His security rests on **tool speed**, not design skill, and he knows it.
The **trainer brand** is a third of Loudhouse's work, a quiet risk.
He has **no big plans**, just building a cushion and basic skills.

steps.text: Practise typography and layout in the evenings
Keep the sticker shop running at about 60 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the gains shared: if a studio can do the same work with half the people, the people pushed out deserve some of that money. I'd post about taxing AI profits to pay for retraining, the usual stuff I'm into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, for the first year or two I'm probably fine, maybe even promoted, because I'm the one who knows the tools. After that, the tools get easy enough that anyone can use them, and my one advantage disappears. Then I'm a junior whose layouts get sent back twice a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Hannah to make me the person who sets up the AI workflows for the whole studio, and push for a small raise for it. I'd put the rest of my time into the skills the tools are worst at, like talking to clients and figuring out what they actually want. And I'd grow the sticker shop, maybe two hundred a month, as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy at the same time. It's like being given a head start in a race where the finish line keeps moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the one who's good with the tools. Doesn't that make you safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a bit. Being good with today's AI tools is like being good with last year's phone. The real question is whether I can become someone clients trust, and I'm not there yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Loudhouse would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucy, who does the copywriting, because the tools already write ad text okay. And Marco, oddly, because his whole value is taste, and if clients decide good-enough taste is fine, he's expensive. I'd worry less about myself than about them, at least at first.

say: I'd say the **gains must be shared** with people pushed out of work.
I'd post about **taxing AI profits** to pay for retraining.
think: For a year or two I'm useful, maybe **promoted**, as the tools person.
Once tools get easy, my advantage goes and my **weak layouts** show.
do: Ask Hannah to make him the studio's **AI workflow** lead, with a small raise.
Build **client skills** the tools are worst at.
Grow the **sticker shop** toward 200 a month.
feel: **Excited** and uneasy, like a head start in a race whose finish keeps moving.
S1.quote: Being good with today's AI tools is like being good with last year's phone.
fieldNote: He sees his **tool advantage** as temporary and says so plainly.
He worries more for **Lucy and Marco** than himself at first.
His politics push for **shared gains**, while his plans are personal and quick.

steps.text: Set up AI ad workflows for all of Loudhouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a basic income now, not in five years. I'd be loud about it, petitions, marches, the lot. If the government doesn't act fast, millions of people like me just fall off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm gone by 2028, and so is Loudhouse. Online shops will make their own ads with AI in an afternoon, and nothing in my job is hands-on, so the robots coming later doesn't help me. Being early with the AI tools just means I'll see my job going a few weeks before everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to grab every bit of cash I can, freelance AI setup work for other agencies on weekends, and get savings from five months to a year. I'd look at jobs where you physically have to be there, like event production or set building for photo shoots, which buys me until about 2031. And I'd join every campaign for a basic income I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Weirdly more scared than people who don't use the tools, because I know exactly how good they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your sticker shop. Does that survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Anyone can make stickers with AI, and the shop would be flooded within months. Maybe the real thing that sells is the stuff you can touch, printed and posted by a person, but I wouldn't bet rent on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents not to worry and then I'd ask if I could move back home for a bit if needed. They live two hours away, in a small town with no design jobs, so it'd be a step back. But it's a safety net most people don't have.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** now, not in five years.
I'd join **petitions and marches**, because millions face a cliff.
think: Loudhouse and my job are **gone by 2028**, as shops make their own ads.
My job has **no hands-on part**, so the robot delay doesn't help.
do: Take weekend **freelance AI setup** work and grow savings toward a year.
Look at **event production** or set building, which lasts until about 2031.
Join every **basic income** campaign he can find.
feel: **Scared**, more than non-users, because he knows how good the tools are.
S2.quote: Being early with the AI tools just means I'll see my job going a few weeks before everyone else.
fieldNote: His **tool knowledge** makes him more frightened, not less.
He reaches for **hands-on work** to borrow three years from the robot delay.
Moving back to his **parents' town** is a safety net he admits he has.

steps.text: Do weekend freelance AI setup work for other agencies
Grow savings from five months to a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up a basic income and retraining, so let's not waste them. I'd be one of the people organising for it, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my design job probably goes by about 2030, before full AGI even arrives, because ad work is the first thing to go. But five years is enough to move into something with people and hands in it. I'd want to be on the other side, helping small firms set the tools up, while that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd start freelancing on AI setup for small shops on weekends and see if it pays. I'd do a short course in video and event production. And I'd save hard, maybe three hundred a month, while I still have a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time buy you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to try things and fail at them, and that's a big deal when you're twenty-seven with five months of savings. I didn't have that in the fast one. I could test the freelancing, see if event work suits me, and still have a job while I do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day. Refusing them would be like refusing to learn to drive because cars are bad for the planet. I'd use them and still argue that the profits should be shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well if we start now, and I'd say it loudly. Basic income, free retraining, shorter weeks, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm thirty-seven when AGI lands, with a second skill built by then. Ten years means I'd probably still lose the design job, but on my terms. The tools would be my job for most of the decade, which suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Loudhouse, ask to lead the AI work, and do evening courses in event production over two or three years. I'd grow the freelance side slowly. I'd keep saving, but I wouldn't panic-save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly curious. It's the version where I get to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this you'd enjoy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes. Ten years of being the person who knows the tools best, getting paid for it, and building something hands-on on the side sounds like a decent run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the gains go to a few companies and everyone else just gets cheaper ads. Ten years doesn't fix that by itself, it just means there's time to fight it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be out of work just as I was getting good. A basic income would help most, and free short courses in hands-on trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether people my age even want design careers any more. Half my friends from college already work in cafés. The AI tools are fun to use, but nobody I know thinks they're building a future on them.

headlineQuote: The AI tools are fun to use, but nobody I know thinks they're building a future on them.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old junior designer** at Loudhouse, making ads for small online shops.
He uses **AI tools every day**, but his basic layout skills are still weak.
His **progressive politics** focus on basic income and taxing AI profits.
He knows his **tool advantage** is temporary and reaches for hands-on event work.
Ten years' warning makes him **curious**, while two years frightens him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing work just as he was getting good.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** and free short courses in **hands-on trades**.
